facts.statement: The federal share of an SS4A grant may not exceed 80 percent; recipients contribute at least 20 percent, from non-federal sources unless a statute authorizes otherwise.
facts.source: Safe Streets and Roads for All FY2026 Notice of Funding Opportunity (U.S. DOT, posted March 27, 2026; PDF attachment SS4A-FY26-NOFO.pdf to opportunity DOT-SS4A-FY26-01), section C.5, PDF page 13. https://apply07.grants.gov/grantsws/rest/opportunity/att/download/350790 | Public Law 117-58, Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, section 24112, Safe Streets and Roads for All Grant Program (135 Stat. 815-817), govinfo.gov, section 24112(e). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-117publ58/html/PLAW-117publ58.htm
facts.supports: The FY 2026 SS4A notice limits the federal share to 80 percent of total eligible project costs and requires a local match of at least 20 percent, generally from non-federal sources; section 24112(e) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act sets the same 80 percent cap.
facts.excerpt: "The Federal share of an SS4A grant may not exceed 80 percent of total eligible SS4A project costs. Recipients are required to contribute a local matching share of no less than 20 percent of total eligible project costs." (NOFO p. 13); "(e) Federal Share.--The Federal share of the cost of an eligible project carried out using a grant provided under the program shall not exceed 80 percent." (IIJA 24112(e))

project-overview.text:
This text is a demonstration prepared by an automated OpenPlan proof run from public sources read on November 14, 2026; Sierra County did not prepare, review, adopt or submit it, and it commits the County to nothing.

The demonstration describes a Planning and Demonstration Grant request under the fiscal year (FY) 2026 Safe Streets and Roads for All (SS4A) notice to develop a comprehensive safety action plan for all public roads in Sierra County, California.

Section 24112 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act names a political subdivision of a State as an eligible entity, and the FY 2026 notice gives counties as an example.

The 2020 Census counted 3,236 residents in Sierra County on 953.2 square miles of land, about 3.4 residents per square mile.

The 2025 Regional Transportation Plan, adopted by the Sierra County Transportation Commission on September 24, 2025, describes a network of State Routes 49 and 89, small sections of US Highway 395 and Interstate 80, and about 400 centerline miles of local roads the County maintains.

The FY 2026 notice closed to applications at 5:00 PM EDT on May 26, 2026, and grants.gov listed no posted or forecasted SS4A opportunity on November 14, 2026, so no open round exists for this text.

The attached safety action plan carries the crash summary, high-injury network, candidate countermeasures and benefit-cost summary the proof run produced.

safety-problem-and-impact.text:
The attached safety action plan reports and ranks the crashes the proof run retrieved.

Where the attached plan draws on the California Crash Reporting System (CCRS), which the California Highway Patrol publishes on the California Open Data Portal, it can include injury crashes: CCRS records each injured person's extent of injury, from fatal through suspected serious, suspected minor and possible injury.

The 2025 Regional Transportation Plan states that, consistent with the County's Local Roadway Safety Plan, the principal contributing factors include driver unfamiliarity with steep mountain highways, frequent wildlife crossings, and winter ice or reduced visibility on high-elevation routes (page 30).

This demonstration assumes two countermeasures from FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures list for up to three of the highest-ranked segments: Enhanced Delineation for Horizontal Curves and Lighting.

For the benefit estimate, this demonstration uses CMF Clearinghouse entry 2438, Install chevron signs on horizontal curves, with a crash modification factor of 0.84 and a four-star quality rating, from Srinivasan and others, Safety Evaluation of Improved Curve Delineation (2009).

OpenPlan's countermeasure list holds no crash modification factor for either countermeasure, and the attached plan says so beside each one; the factor used here is this demonstration's own reading of the CMF Clearinghouse.

That factor applies to fatal and injury (KABC) non-intersection crashes on rural, two-lane undivided roads carrying 261 to 14,790 vehicles a day, studied in Washington State with 1993 to 2007 data, and it assumes no curve sign was there before.

The benefit-cost analysis applies it to every death recorded on one treated segment, including any at an intersection or away from a curve, and assumes deaths fall by the same share the study found for all injury crashes combined; Lighting enters with no factor and no cost.

equity-and-underserved-communities.text:
The FY 2026 SS4A notice defines an Area of Persistent Poverty, and uses the same definition for an underserved community, as a county with 20 percent or more of its population in poverty over the 30 years before November 15, 2021, or a census tract with a poverty rate of at least 20 percent in the 2014–2018 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year data.

Sierra County holds one census tract in that data series, Census Tract 100, where the 2014–2018 ACS (table B17001) estimates 241 of 2,903 people, 8.3 percent, below the poverty level, so the tract does not meet the tract test.

This demonstration did not test the county measure, which needs the 1990 and 2000 decennial census and the Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates.

The 2020 Census counted 3,196 of the County's 3,236 residents, 98.8 percent, in rural territory.

How the action plan reaches people who walk, bike, ride transit or drive the County's roads, and which communities it names, are decisions for Sierra County; this demonstration makes none of them.

engagement-and-collaboration.text:
No public engagement took place for this demonstration.

The two comments and the staff review summarized in Appendix E were entered by the automated proof run to test the comment, moderation and review screens; no resident, staff member or partner agency wrote them, and they are not evidence of public opinion in Sierra County.

Table 1 of the FY 2026 SS4A notice calls for engagement with the public, stakeholders and partners, analysis of what that engagement yields, inclusion of overlapping jurisdictions, and coordination with other governmental plans.

The County's Regional Transportation Plan web page lists past community outreach sessions for that plan at the Downieville Community Hall and the Loyalton Senior Center.

The County's Transportation Commission web page describes the Sierra County Transportation Commission as the regional transportation planning agency since 1972, with members appointed by the City of Loyalton and the County.

The 2025 Regional Transportation Plan's Policy 3.1.1 calls for annual interface with Caltrans (page 42).

Which partners to invite, and how and when to engage the public, are decisions for Sierra County; this demonstration makes none of them.

implementation-and-capacity.text:
Who manages the grant, who prepares the action plan, the schedule from award to adoption and the body that adopts the plan are decisions for Sierra County; this demonstration does not make them.

The FY 2026 SS4A notice expects a period of performance between 24 months and five years and caps it at five years.

Its Table 1 lists the components a qualifying action plan includes: leadership commitment and goal setting, a planning structure, safety analysis, engagement and collaboration, policy and process changes, strategy and project selections, and progress and transparency.

The attached safety action plan covers part of the safety analysis component, crash locations and severity from the proof run's retrieval and a ranked high-injury network, and it supplies no leadership commitment, planning structure or policy review.

The notice states that the safety analysis should include all roadways within the jurisdiction, without regard to ownership, to the extent practical.

In Sierra County that includes the state highways and about 400 centerline miles of local roads the County maintains, according to the 2025 Regional Transportation Plan (page 25).

This demonstration assumes chevron signs on one treated segment as an example item for the benefit-cost analysis; that choice is this demonstration's, not the County's.

Enhanced Delineation for Horizontal Curves and Lighting both appear on FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures list page in its Internet Archive capture of November 4, 2026, read that way because FHWA's site refused automated reads on November 14, 2026.

FHWA's Lighting page states that research indicates continuous lighting on both rural and urban highways has an established safety benefit for motorized vehicles.

budget-narrative.text:
The budget amount, the local match and its source are decisions for Sierra County; this demonstration sets none of them, and the attached budget document holds no cost estimate.

The FY 2026 SS4A notice limits the federal share to 80 percent of total eligible project costs and requires a local match of at least 20 percent, generally from non-federal sources; section 24112(e) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act sets the same 80 percent cap.

The notice expects Planning and Demonstration Grants of $100,000 to $5,000,000.

The one cost in this packet is the benefit-cost analysis's capital cost, which this demonstration assumes: 12 one-post roadside signs on one treated segment at $552.85 each, the weighted average unit price of 2025 awarded bids statewide for Caltrans item 820840, Roadside Sign - One Post, for a total of $6,634 in 2025 bid dollars.

The sign count is a planning assumption, not a field inventory of curves, and the price covers that one bid item only: Caltrans pays for sign panels separately (2023 Standard Specifications, section 82-3.04), and traffic control, design and contingency are not counted.

The analysis enters the cost as one outlay in its first analysis year, without escalation from 2025 dollars.

Set against one avoided death, that cost yields a very large ratio in the attached plan; the ratio rests on one segment, an assumed factor and an incomplete cost, and it does not show that the project is cost-effective.
